Spartan Electric: Design, Build, and Deployment of a First-Generation Catamaran for the PEP26 Uncrewed Open
Division
Abstract
This paper presents the design, development, and systems integration of the Spartan Electric, a twin-hull catamaranconfiguration uncrewed surface vessel (USV) purpose-built for the 2025–2026 Promoting Electric Propulsion (PEP)
Workforce Development Competition, organized by the American Society of Naval Engineers (ASNE) and
sponsored by the Office of Naval Research (ONR). Competing in the Uncrewed Open Division, the vessel must
autonomously or remotely traverse a two-mile oval course in the Elizabeth River at Portsmouth City Park, Virginia,
while carrying a removable 60-pound payload, all under a 55.5-volt electrical ceiling. As a first-year entrant, our team
confronted the challenge of building an entirely original electric propulsion system from the ground up: hull
fabrication, dual-motor powertrain, lithium-ion energy storage, remote-control architecture, and Pixhawk-based
telemetry, without the benefit of inherited designs, tooling, or institutional knowledge. This article documents
background research that informed our design philosophy, the naval architecture calculations and simulations that
shaped the catamaran hull geometry, the engineering rationale behind every major subsystem, the build and testing
processes employed, the risk identification and mitigation strategies adopted, and the lessons learned throughout a
demanding development cycle. The paper concludes with a forward-looking discussion of autonomy integration,
object detection, and autopiloting, solar-assisted energy harvesting, and advanced hull materials that the team intends
to pursue in subsequent competition years. The Spartan Electric represents not merely a competition entry but a
comprehensive educational platform through which team members have acquired professional competencies in
marine engineering, electrical systems design, embedded controls, and project management.
Keywords: electric propulsion, catamaran, unmanned surface vessel, PEP competition, lithium-ion battery, Pixhawk,
Raspberry Pi, naval architecture, collegiate engineering

to the growing body of student-authored literature on practical electric propulsion.
The structure of this paper is as follows. Section 2 states the aims and objectives that guided the project. Section 3
reviews the background research that informed our key design decisions. Section 4 describes the methodology,
including hull design, propulsion, power storage, controls, and telemetry. Section 5 details the design considerations,

prospects and planned innovations. Section 8 provides the conclusion.

2. Aim and Objectives
The overarching aim of the Spartan Electric project is to design, fabricate, and successfully race a catamaranconfiguration uncrewed electric vessel that meets all PEP26 Uncrewed Open Division requirements while
maximizing reliability, efficiency, and ease of deployment.
The specific objectives derived from this aim are:
1. Hull performance. Design a twin-hull catamaran with low wave-making resistance at the target
displacement, incorporating adequate reserve buoyancy (trapped air via watertight compartments and closedcell foam) to remain afloat even if fully swamped, and a towing bridle connecting both hulls for safe retrieval.
2. Propulsion efficiency. Develop a dual-motor propulsion system-one motor per hull-that converts stored
electrical energy into thrust with minimal mechanical and hydrodynamic losses, using individually sourced
components (motor, shaft, propeller) rather than a pre-built kit, in compliance with PEP rules.
3. Energy management. Specify and integrate two lithium-ion battery packs (two in one hull only) with
appropriate battery management systems (BMS), fusing, and a main-power disconnect to satisfy the 55.5 V
/ 500 Ah limits and the safety requirements of the competition.
4. Remote control and telemetry. Implement a reliable remote-control link and a Pixhawk-based telemetry
system providing real-time GPS position, heading, speed, battery voltage, and current data to the shore
operator, supporting both manual piloting and future autonomous waypoint navigation.
5. Rapid deployment. Engineer the vessel and its launching procedures so that the craft can move from trailer
to open water within the mandated five-minute window at the boat ramp.
6. Documentation excellence. Produce a white paper and video presentation that clearly narrates the
background research, design rationale, build process, subsystem testing, and risk mitigation, targeting full
marks under the PEP26 rubric.

3. Background Research
3.1 Electric Propulsion in the Maritime Sector

Electric propulsion for watercraft dates to the 1830s, when Moritz von Jacobi demonstrated an electromagnetically
driven paddle boat on the Neva River. However, the technology remained marginal until advances in power
electronics, permanent-magnet motor design, and lithium-ion battery chemistry converged in the early 21st century

pages.text:
The advantages of electric propulsion are particularly pronounced for small uncrewed vessels: the absence of exhaust
emissions, reduced acoustic signature, lower vibration levels improving sensor performance, simplified drivetrain
with fewer moving parts, and the possibility of regenerative braking in reversing maneuvers. These benefits align
closely with the strategic interests of the Office of Naval Research (ONR), which sponsors PEP as part of its broader
workforce development portfolio aimed at ensuring the United States possesses the engineering talent base to design
and maintain next-generation naval platforms.
3.2 Catamaran Hull Form Selection
The choice of hull configuration is perhaps the single most consequential design decision for any vessel. For our
Spartan Electric, we evaluated three candidate hull forms: a conventional monohull, a catamaran (twin hull), and a
trimaran (triple hull). The selection criteria included hydrodynamic resistance at the target speed, transverse stability
(particularly relevant for an uncrewed craft carrying a 60-pound payload in potentially choppy river conditions),
available deck area for component mounting, manufacturability with available tools and materials, ease of launching
within the five-minute constraint and various mechanical advantages that directly impact efficiency and speed.
The catamaran emerged as the preferred configuration for several reasons:
•
•
•
•
•

Stability & Weight: The wide beam provides high initial stability without needing a heavy ballast keel (dead
weight), preventing capsizing while keeping the vessel light.
Efficiency: Two slender hulls reduce wave-making resistance and drag. When hulls are spaced correctly to
avoid interference, this significantly lowers energy consumption - crucial for battery-powered racing.
Optimal Loading: Splitting the 60lb payload between both hulls preserves the vessel’s trim and minimizes
the wet surface area, keeping the boat balanced and fast.
Endurance: Improved weight distribution and reduced drag allow for higher sustained speeds and better
handling over long distances (2+ miles).
Layout: The bridge deck offers superior space for component integration and structural efficiency compared
to a monohull.

3.3 Lithium-Ion Battery Technology
Lithium-ion cells offer the highest gravimetric energy density among commercially available rechargeable
chemistries, typically 150–250 Wh/kg at the cell level depending on cathode chemistry (NMC, NCA, LFP). For
marine applications, lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4, or LFP) is increasingly favored due to its superior thermal
stability, longer cycle life, and lower risk of thermal runaway compared with nickel-based chemistries-advantages
that outweigh its moderately lower energy density of approximately 120–160 Wh/kg (Scrosati & Garche, 2010).
The PEP rules impose a hard ceiling of 55.5 V and 500 Ah. Our LFP packs, configured as 14S (14 cells in series,
yielding a nominal voltage of 44.8 V and a fully charged voltage of 51.1 V), sit comfortably within this envelope
while providing a useful capacity of approximately 20 Ah each, adequate for the energy budget calculated in Section
5. Each pack includes a dedicated battery management system (BMS) that monitors individual cell voltages, pack
temperature, and state of charge, providing cell balancing during charging and over-discharge protection during
operation.

Uncrewed surface vessels require a reliable command-and-control link between the shore operator and the craft. For
PEP26 Uncrewed Open Division, the baseline operating mode is remote control (RC): a human operator on shore or
aboard a support vessel steers the craft using a handheld transmitter. The PEP rules additionally require a kill switch
that ceases all high-voltage electrical systems when engaged, and for teams pursuing autonomy, a fail-safe that
engages the kill switch when GPS data is missing or corrupted.

We selected the Pixhawk open-source autopilot platform as the telemetry and (future) navigation computer for
the Spartan Electric. The Pixhawk hardware, based on the STM32 microcontroller family, integrates an inertial
measurement unit (IMU), barometer, magnetometer, and GPS receiver, and runs the ArduPilot firmware stack, which
supports both manual RC pass-through and autonomous waypoint navigation. In our current configuration, the
Pixhawk serves primarily as a telemetry hub: it receives GPS position and heading data, reads battery voltage and
current via an analog power module, and transmits this information over a 915 MHz radio link to a ground station
running Mission Planner software. This architecture provides the shore operator with situational awareness during
the race, knowing the craft's speed, position on the course, and remaining battery energy, and lays the groundwork
for a future upgrade to GPS-guided autonomous operation.

4. Methodology
4.1 Hull Design and Fabrication
The hull design process began with a parametric study using basic naval architecture principles. The target
displacement for each hull was determined by summing the estimated component weights (motor, battery, payload,
structure) and adding a 15% design margin for growth and contingency. This yielded a per-hull displacement of
approximately 25 kg (55 lb), giving a total vessel displacement of roughly 50 kg (110 lb) when unladen, and 77 kg
(170 lb) when carrying the 60-pound (27.2 kg) payload.
We selected a V-bottom hull form (rather than flat or round bilge, so it cuts through the water and waves more
cleanly and behaves better at speed and in waves) with a length-to-beam ratio of approximately 5:1 for each individual
hull (For each hull, its waterline length is about eight times its width. That makes each hull long and slender rather
than short and chunky), balancing low wave-making resistance (which favors long, slender hulls) against structural
stiffness and internal volume. The hull length was set at 6.4 feet per hull, with a maximum beam of 1.4 feet. Hull
separation (side-to-side) was fixed at 7.5 inches, a compromise between minimizing wave interference (which favors
wider separation) and limiting the overall beam for ease of transport and launching.

The core structural material of the vessel is wood, with Sande plywood used for the hull panels, bulkheads, and deck
components, while dimensional timber was used for stringers, frames, and localized reinforcements. Southern Yellow
Pine dimensional lumber was used for the framing members due to its adequate strength, availability, good bonding
performance with epoxy adhesives, and ease of machining and assembly. The moisture content of the wood was
controlled before construction, and all wood components were sealed and encapsulated to prevent moisture intrusion
and long-term deterioration. PVC pipes were also used as hull bottom stiffeners in the central section of each hull to
provide additional structural support and reduce bottom panel deflection under load. These pipes acted as lightweight
internal stiffeners that helped distribute loads along the hull bottom and improve overall structural rigidity. The sealed
PVC pipes also contributed minor additional buoyancy while keeping the structure lightweight, and the stiffeners
were bonded into the wooden hull structure to ensure proper load transfer between the hull skin and internal framing.

The protective composite skin consists of woven roving fiberglass cloth combined with an epoxy resin system. Epoxy
resin was selected instead of polyester or vinyl ester resin because epoxy provides stronger adhesion to wood fibers,
lower shrinkage during curing, and better long-term moisture barrier performance, making it more suitable for woodcomposite boat construction. The objective of this approach is to combine the stiffness, workability, and costeffectiveness of marine wood with the moisture barrier, abrasion resistance, and durability of fiberglass-reinforced
resin. By combining these materials, the structure benefits from the strength and ease of fabrication of wood while
relying on fiberglass and resin to protect the structure from water and environmental damage.

Applying fiber glass on Hulls
A major design consideration was the waterproofing strategy. Every exposed wood surface was sealed, and the hull
exterior was fully sheathed in fiberglass and epoxy, while interior bilge areas and high-humidity zones were also
epoxy-coated. All penetrations, including fasteners, drains, fittings, and rudder fittings, were sealed to prevent water
from entering the wood structure. The main objective of this waterproofing strategy was to prevent direct water
ingress into the wood and long-term moisture accumulation within the structure. The fiberglass laminate schedule
was also designed to balance impact and abrasion resistance, overall hull stiffness, local reinforcement at high-load
points, and overall vessel weight, with lighter fiberglass layers used in low-stress areas and heavier reinforcement
applied near high-load regions such as keel areas, beam landing areas, and slamming zones.
Environmental effects such as moisture and thermal cycling were also considered, as temperature and humidity
changes can cause expansion and contraction differences between wood and the cured fiberglass laminate. These
effects were mitigated by maintaining continuous epoxy coatings, applying protective topcoats, sealing all end-grain
surfaces, and ensuring regular inspection of coating integrity. Damage tolerance and repairability were also
considered so that repairs can be performed using common marine epoxy and fiberglass repair methods, and access
to internal sides of critical structural areas was provided where possible to simplify maintenance and repair operations.

surfaces with epoxy before fiberglass application, avoiding dry spots, air entrapment, and resin starvation during

material cost compared to full composite construction, good stiffness-to-cost ratio, and easier shaping and repair,

applied near high-load regions such as keel areas, beam landing areas, and slamming zones.

Environmental effects such as moisture and thermal cycling were also considered, as temperature and humidity
changes can cause expansion and contraction differences between wood and the cured fiberglass laminate. These
effects were mitigated by maintaining continuous epoxy coatings, applying protective topcoats, sealing all end-grain
surfaces, and ensuring regular inspection of coating integrity. Damage tolerance and repairability were also
considered so that repairs can be performed using common marine epoxy and fiberglass repair methods, and access
to internal sides of critical structural areas was provided where possible to simplify maintenance and repair operations.

During construction, several quality control measures were implemented, including pre-coating absorbent wood
surfaces with epoxy before fiberglass application, avoiding dry spots, air entrapment, and resin starvation during
lamination, and maintaining proper curing conditions. Surface finishing was completed before applying protective
coatings, and quality checks included visual inspection for pinholes and voids as well as tap testing in suspect areas
for possible delamination. Overall, the wood and fiberglass construction method presents advantages such as lower
material cost compared to full composite construction, good stiffness-to-cost ratio, and easier shaping and repair,
although it requires careful sealing to prevent moisture ingress and proper resin control to avoid unnecessary weight
increase.

leakage was observed during the test, indicating that the fiberglass coating and waterproofing execution were

Each pack is secured to the hull structure with cut-out wood on each side. A buckle is added to retain the battery in a
capsize event (PEP Rule 8).
A main power disconnect switch (PEP Rule 7) is mounted on the upper surface of each hull, accessible without tools,
through which all current to the propulsion system in that hull must travel. Moving either switch to OFF immediately
ceases all high-voltage electrical activity in the respective hull. The location of each disconnect is marked with a
bright orange label visible from above and from the waterline and is documented in our safety checklist for race-day
inspection.
For the 24–55 V operating range, each hull includes a 60A ANL-type fuse in-line between the battery and the ESC
(PEP Rule 9), sized to protect the 10 AWG silicone-jacketed wiring that constitutes the high-voltage bus. The fuse is
housed in a waterproof fuse holder accessible through a deck hatch.
4.4 Controls and Communication
The "brain" of our craft is a Pixhawk flight controller running ArduRover. We integrated two Cytron MD30A motor
drivers to translate the Pixhawk’s logic-level commands into high-current power. We utilized a modern ExpressLRS
(ELRS) 2.4GHz system to route both ultra-low-latency manual control and high-speed MAVLink telemetry through
a single RF link.
The control architecture of the Spartan Electric is organized into three layers:
1. Operator layer. A 2.4 GHz frequency-hopping spread-spectrum (FHSS) RC transmitter provides the
primary control link. The transmitter has been range-tested to over 1.5 km line-of-sight, well beyond the
maximum distance from the shore to any point on the two-mile oval course. The transmitter outputs throttle
and steering commands, which are mixed into individual motor speed commands by the receiver's built-in
mixing function.
2. Vehicle layer. The RC receiver passes PWM signals either directly to the two ESCs (manual mode) or via
the Pixhawk autopilot (assisted/autonomous mode). A two-position switch on the transmitter selects the
mode. In manual mode, the operator has direct low-latency control of the motors. In autonomous mode (not
yet activated for PEP26 but architecturally supported), the Pixhawk follows a pre-programmed waypoint
mission.
3. Telemetry layer. The Pixhawk transmits telemetry data-GPS coordinates, speed over ground, heading, roll,
pitch, battery voltage, battery current, and remaining capacity estimate-over a dedicated 915 MHz SiK radio
link to a laptop running Mission Planner ground station software. Pixhawk also logs all sensor data to an
onboard microSD card at 25 Hz for post-race analysis.
4.4.1 Build and Integration
Fabricating the control system required strict attention to power segregation and precise signal formatting to protect
the embedded logic from the extreme electrical loads of the propulsion system.
1. Power Segregation and Logic Isolation: Electric brushed motors inherently create massive voltage spikes
and severe voltage sag under heavy acceleration. To prevent these fluctuations from browning out or resetting
the flight controller, the control electronics are completely isolated from the main propulsion power rail. The
Cytron MD30A drivers are fed directly from the raw 12V battery array. In contrast, the Pixhawk and the
ELRS receiver are powered entirely via a dedicated 5V Battery Eliminator Circuit (BEC). This buck
converter acts as an electrical firewall, delivering a perfectly regulated 5V stream regardless of the voltage
sag on the 12V rail.

2. Actuation Wiring and Skid-Steer Mixing: For actuation, the Pixhawk’s servo output rails were wired
directly to the Cytron PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) and DIR (Direction) input terminals. Rather than
utilizing external hardware mixers, ArduRover’s internal skid-steering parameters were configured to
natively mix throttle and yaw inputs, translating a single joystick vector into independent, variable-voltage
left and right motor commands.
3. The Telemetry Pipeline: A RadioMaster TX16S transmitter equipped with an internal ELRS module serves
as the primary ground controller. The onboard ELRS receiver was integrated via its TX/RX serial pads
directly into the Pixhawk’s TELEM2 port, establishing the physical bridge for wireless data transmission to
the Mission Planner ground control station.
The kill-switch functionality is implemented as follows. The ArduRover firmware is configured with strict, automated
fail-safes. The Pixhawk actively monitors the RC heartbeat. If the signal is lost for more than 2.0 seconds, the flight
controller automatically overrides the current mission and transitions into "Hold" mode, instantly commanding a
1500µs neutral PWM signal to the Cytron drivers, stopping the vessel dead in the water until the RF link is reacquired.
A Battery Failsafe was configured within the ArduRover logic. The Pixhawk utilizes an analog-to-digital converter
(ADC) via the power module to monitor real-time main battery voltage.
The BATT_LOW_VOLT parameter is programmed to a conservative threshold. If crossed, it triggers an audible and
visual alarm on the Mission Planner ground station HUD, alerting the operator to reduce throttle thereby saving
enough power for the rest of the mission
A dedicated channel on the RC transmitter is assigned to a spring-loaded switch. When this switch is activated, the
Pixhawk commands both ESCs to zero throttle and asserts a relay that opens the main-power contactor, disconnecting
the batteries from the high-voltage bus. The same relay is wired to the Pixhawk's GPS-fail-safe output: if GPS fix is
lost for more than five seconds, the relay opens automatically, satisfying PEP Rule 21 for teams pursuing autonomy
credits.
4.5 Payload Integration
The 60-pound payload is divided into two 30-pound sandbags, one placed in each hull's central payload bay. The
payload bays are located at the longitudinal center of buoyancy of the hull, so that loading and unloading the payload
does not change the vessel's trim angle. The sandbags rest on a non-skid mat and are retained by a Velcro strap across
the top of the bay. The deck hatch above each payload bay is secured with quarter-turn fasteners for rapid removal
and inspection by the dockside judge during the five-minute launch window. This arrangement satisfies the PEP
requirement that the payload be a unified 30-pound whole per hull and be quickly removable.

Throughout testing, we maintained a detailed engineering log documenting every trial, anomaly, root-cause analysis,
and corrective action. This log informed many of the design iterations described in the following section.
5. Design Considerations
5.1 Resistance and Powering Analysis
Estimating the total resistance of the catamaran at the design speed was critical for sizing the propulsion system and
the battery. We decomposed total resistance into frictional resistance (calculated using the ITTC 1957 model-ship
correlation line), residuary (wave-making) resistance (estimated from Holtrop-Mennen regression for slender hulls),
and interference resistance between the two hulls (estimated as a fraction of the monohull wave-making resistance,
based on the hull separation-to-length ratio, following the methodology of Insel and Molland, 1992).
At the design speed of 3.5 m/s (Froude number Fn ≈ 0.29 based on individual hull waterline length), the estimated
total resistance is approximately 25 N per hull, or 50 N for the catamaran. The effective power is therefore:
P_E = R_T × V = 50 N × 3.5 m/s = 175 W
Accounting for propulsive efficiency (estimated at 55%, comprising propeller open-water efficiency of 65%, relativerotative efficiency of 98%, hull efficiency of 1.02, and shaft mechanical efficiency of 90%) and ESC/motor electrical
efficiency (estimated at 85%), the total electrical power draw from the batteries is:
P_elec = P_E / (η_prop × η_elec) = 175 / (0.55 × 0.85) ≈ 374 W per hull pair
For the two-mile (3,219 m) course at 3.5 m/s, the estimated race time is approximately 920 seconds, or 15.3 minutes.
The total energy consumed is:
E = P_elec × t = 374 W × 920 s ≈ 344 Wh
With a total battery capacity of 1,792 Wh and a recommended maximum depth of discharge of 80% (to preserve
battery cycle life), the usable energy is 1,434 Wh-providing a safety factor of approximately 4.2 over the estimated
race energy requirement. This generous margin accommodates the uncertainties inherent in resistance prediction for
a first-build hull, as well as the additional energy consumed during maneuvering at the turns of the oval course and
during the launch and recovery phases.

5.2 Structural Analysis

pages.text:
The crossbeam frame connecting the two hulls is subject to bending and torsional loads arising from differential wave
loading on the two hulls. We estimated the worst-case bending moment by assuming one hull rides a wave crest while
the other is in a trough, with a wave height of 0.3 m (representative of the sheltered Elizabeth River conditions at
Portsmouth City Park). The resulting bending moment on the crossbeam is approximately 200 N·m. Using standard
beam bending theory, the selected 25 mm × 25 mm × 3 mm wall 6061-T6 aluminum square tube (moment of inertia
I ≈ 2.1 × 10⁴ mm⁴, yield stress σ_y = 276 MPa) has a bending stress of approximately 60 MPa under this load,
providing a safety factor of 4.6 against yield. Torsional stiffness was verified by applying a differential vertical load
to the hull-attachment flanges on a bench fixture and measuring the angular deflection, which was less than 0.5
degrees at the design load.
5.3 Thermal Management
During sustained full-throttle operation, the BLDC motors and ESCs generate waste heat that must be dissipated to
avoid thermal derating or shutdown. The motors are mounted at the aft end of each hull with direct contact to the hull
shell, which is in turn cooled by the surrounding water-a highly effective heat sink. The ESCs are mounted on an
aluminum plate that conducts heat to the hull via a thermal pad. Temperature sensors bonded to the motor windings,
and the ESC MOSFETs feed data to the Pixhawk telemetry stream, allowing the shore operator to monitor thermal
conditions in real time. During pool testing at continuous full throttle, motor winding temperatures stabilized at
approximately 65°C and ESC temperatures at approximately 55°C, both well within their rated limits of 120°C and
100°C, respectively.
5.4 Waterproofing and Buoyancy
For an uncrewed vessel, waterproofing is not merely a convenience but a survival requirement: there is no crew to
bail, and the PEP rules mandate positive buoyancy even when fully swamped (Rule 19). Our waterproofing strategy
is defense-in-depth:
•

First line: The hull itself, with all through-hull penetrations (shaft tubes, wiring glands, antenna
feedthroughs) sealed with marine-grade silicone sealant and hose clamps.

•

Second line: The forward buoyancy compartment, filled with closed-cell polyurethane foam (density 32
kg/m³), which provides approximately 15 kg of buoyancy force per hull even if the remainder of the hull is
flooded.

•

Third line: The battery box and electronics tray are individually sealed and have their own positive buoyancy
(the battery box floats due to the foam lining, and the electronics tray is enclosed in a waterproof Pelicanstyle case).

We verified positive buoyancy by deliberately swamping a hull with a garden hose while loaded with the battery and
payload: the hull settled to just below the deck line and remained stable, with the foam providing sufficient reserve
buoyancy to keep the crossbeam frame above water.
5.5 Launch Procedure Optimization

competition. Our launch procedure was rehearsed repeatedly and optimized as follows:

The crossbeam frame connecting the two hulls is subject to bending and torsional loads arising from differential wave
loading on the two hulls. We estimated the worst-case bending moment by assuming one hull rides a wave crest while
the other is in a trough, with a wave height of 0.3 m (representative of the sheltered Elizabeth River conditions at
Portsmouth City Park). The resulting bending moment on the crossbeam is approximately 200 N·m. Using standard
beam bending theory, the selected 25 mm × 25 mm × 3 mm wall 6061-T6 aluminum square tube (moment of inertia
I ≈ 2.1 × 10⁴ mm⁴, yield stress σ_y = 276 MPa) has a bending stress of approximately 60 MPa under this load,
providing a safety factor of 4.6 against yield. Torsional stiffness was verified by applying a differential vertical load
to the hull-attachment flanges on a bench fixture and measuring the angular deflection, which was less than 0.5
degrees at the design load.

5.3 Thermal Management

During sustained full-throttle operation, the BLDC motors and ESCs generate waste heat that must be dissipated to
avoid thermal derating or shutdown. The motors are mounted at the aft end of each hull with direct contact to the hull
shell, which is in turn cooled by the surrounding water-a highly effective heat sink. The ESCs are mounted on an
aluminum plate that conducts heat to the hull via a thermal pad. Temperature sensors bonded to the motor windings,
and the ESC MOSFETs feed data to the Pixhawk telemetry stream, allowing the shore operator to monitor thermal
conditions in real time. During pool testing at continuous full throttle, motor winding temperatures stabilized at
approximately 65°C and ESC temperatures at approximately 55°C, both well within their rated limits of 120°C and
100°C, respectively.

5.4 Waterproofing and Buoyancy

For an uncrewed vessel, waterproofing is not merely a convenience but a survival requirement: there is no crew to
bail, and the PEP rules mandate positive buoyancy even when fully swamped (Rule 19). Our waterproofing strategy
is defense-in-depth:

    •   First line: The hull itself, with all through-hull penetrations (shaft tubes, wiring glands, antenna
        feedthroughs) sealed with marine-grade silicone sealant and hose clamps.

    •   Second line: The forward buoyancy compartment, filled with closed-cell polyurethane foam (density 32
        kg/m³), which provides approximately 15 kg of buoyancy force per hull even if the remainder of the hull is
        flooded.

    •   Third line: The battery box and electronics tray are individually sealed and have their own positive buoyancy
        (the battery box floats due to the foam lining, and the electronics tray is enclosed in a waterproof Pelican-
        style case).

We verified positive buoyancy by deliberately swamping a hull with a garden hose while loaded with the battery and
payload: the hull settled to just below the deck line and remained stable, with the foam providing sufficient reserve
buoyancy to keep the crossbeam frame above water.

6.3 Lessons Learned from Testing
Several significant issues were identified and resolved during the testing phases:
1. Shaft vibration. During initial pool trials, a resonant vibration was observed at approximately 2,200 RPM,
traced to a slight misalignment between the motor pulley and the propeller shaft pulley. The fix was to
machine a precision alignment jig and re-mount the motor, eliminating the vibration.
2. Telemetry dropouts. The 915 MHz telemetry radio experienced intermittent dropouts when the vessel was
oriented with the hull between the antenna and the ground station. Relocating the SiK radio antenna to the
top of a vertical mast on the crossbeam resolved the issue.
3. ESC overheating during low-speed operation. At very low throttle settings, the ESC's switching losses
became proportionally significant, causing the MOSFET temperature to rise. We programmed a minimum
throttle threshold below which the ESC cuts to zero, preventing prolonged low-current operation in the
inefficient regime.
4. Payload bay flooding during wave impacts. The original deck hatch design allowed spray to enter the
payload bay through the quarter-turn fastener holes. We added neoprene gaskets and silicone-sealed the
fastener penetrations, eliminating the leak path.

7.1 Autonomous Navigation

demonstrated levels of autonomous operation. The kill-switch fail-safe on GPS loss is already implemented,
satisfying PEP Rule 21.
7.2 Solar-Assisted Energy Harvesting
PEP rules permit solar power and other renewable systems onboard for battery recharging (Rule 4). We plan to install
a lightweight, flexible solar panel array on the crossbeam deck area. Even a modest 100 W panel, operating at an
average of 60% capacity during a sunny race day, could contribute approximately 60 Wh over a one-hour period
enough to extend range or allow the vessel to recover energy between heats. The solar charge controller would
integrate with the existing BMS, and the Pixhawk telemetry would display solar input power alongside battery state.
7.3 Advanced Hull Materials
The current fiberglass hulls, while functional and economical, are heavier than optimal. Future iterations will explore
carbon-fiber or Kevlar-reinforced composite layups, which could reduce hull weight by 30–40% for the same
structural strength. A lighter hull directly translates to lower displacement, reduced wet surface area, and lower
resistance-a virtuous cycle that improves both speed and endurance. We also plan to investigate hull surface
treatments (hydrophobic coatings, micro-textured surfaces) that reduce frictional resistance.
7.4 Hydrofoil Integration
At higher speeds, the catamaran could benefit from retractable surface-piercing hydrofoils that lift the hulls partially
or fully out of the water, dramatically reducing hydrodynamic resistance. While this is a longer-term goal requiring
significant design and testing effort, the wide beam and structural rigidity of the catamaran platform make it a suitable
candidate for foil-assisted operation.
7.5 Enhanced Telemetry and Data Analytics
Future development will incorporate additional sensors-water-speed paddle wheel, hull-mounted strain gauges, motor
current transducers with high-frequency sampling-feeding a real-time performance dashboard displayed to the shore
operator. Post-race data analytics, using machine-learning techniques applied to the Pixhawk log files, will identify
optimal throttle profiles for each segment of the course (straight legs versus turns) to minimize total race time within
the energy budget.
7.6 Modular Payload System
To support research collaborations beyond the PEP competition, we plan to design a standardized payload interface
on the crossbeam deck that can accommodate environmental monitoring instruments (water quality sensors, acoustic
recorders) or hydrographic survey equipment. This would transform the Spartan Electric from a competition platform
into a versatile research USV capable of supporting faculty-led research projects in coastal and riverine environments.
8. Conclusion
The Spartan Electric catamaran represents the culmination of a 4-month-long, ground-up engineering effort by a
first-time PEP team. From an empty workshop to an integrated, tested, and race-ready uncrewed surface vessel, the
project demanded and delivered competencies spanning naval architecture, composite fabrication, electrical power
systems, embedded controls, and project management. Every subsystem of the craft - twin fiberglass-coated hulls,
dual BLDC motor drivetrains with timing-belt reduction, LiFePO4 battery packs with BMS, differential-thrust
steering, RC control with Pixhawk telemetry, and a structured payload integration was researched, designed,
fabricated, and validated by the team, using no pre-built motor assemblies or commercial kits, in full compliance with
PEP26 rules.

The catamaran configuration proved to be an excellent choice for the Uncrewed Open Division, offering high
stability, low wave-making resistance at the design of Froude number, inherent propulsion redundancy, and
symmetric payload distribution. The resistance and power analysis predict a race time of approximately 15 minutes
for the two-mile course at 3.5 m/s, with a battery energy safety factor exceeding 4:1, providing ample margin for the
uncertainties inherent in a first-generation design. The crossbeam structure has been analyzed and tested to a safety
factor exceeding 4.5 against yield under the worst-case wave-loading scenario.
Risk management was embedded throughout the project lifecycle. A formal risk register tracked hazards from hull
fabrication through race-day operations, and each risk was paired with specific mitigation measures that were tested
during the phased development process. The lessons learned during testing, from shaft vibration to telemetry dropouts
to deck hatch leakage, were documented, analyzed, and resolved, demonstrating the iterative engineering process that
is central to the PEP competition's educational mission.
Looking ahead, the Spartan Electric platform has been deliberately architected for growth. The Pixhawk autopilot,
already installed and telemetry-functional, is ready for activation in autonomous waypoint mode, opening the door
to the PEP Autonomy Division in future years. Solar energy harvesting, advanced composite hulls, hydrofoil
integration, enhanced data analytics, and a modular research payload interface are all on the development roadmap,
ensuring that the vessel will continue to evolve as a vehicle for both competition and learning.
Perhaps most importantly, the Spartan Electric project has achieved its workforce-development mission. Each team
member has gained direct, hands-on experience in the engineering disciplines required by the naval enterprise.
Members who began the year having never laid up a fiberglass panel, soldered a high-current connector, or configured
a flight controller are now confident in these skills - and eager to apply them, whether in the next PEP competition
or in careers across the maritime, defense, and energy industries. The PEP competition, supported by ASNE and
ONR, provides an unparalleled framework for this kind of experiential learning, and we are proud to contribute to its
growing community of student engineers.

Research (ONR) for organizing and funding the PEP Workforce Development Competition. We thank John Duvall
for motivating us, providing us with everything that we needed for the project, and for his guidance throughout the
design process. He played a major role in the commencement of the project, continuation, and completion of the
